title: Expenses

objectives.text: Sort expenses into fixed, variable and occasional categories.
Explain the difference between a need and a want when money is tight.
Use a simple spending record to find money that can be redirected to savings.

explanation: An expense is money that goes out. Fixed expenses stay roughly the same every month, such as rent, a loan instalment or a phone plan. Variable expenses move with your choices, such as groceries, transport and eating out. Occasional expenses appear a few times a year, such as insurance premiums, festival spending or a medical bill.

RBI's financial awareness material puts the relationship plainly: expenditure equals income minus saving. That ordering matters. If you spend first and save what is left, saving usually loses. If you set aside a portion of income before spending, the rest becomes your spending limit.

Separating needs from wants is not about guilt. It is about ordering. A need keeps your life running: rent, food, medicines, school fees, minimum loan payments. A want improves life but can wait a month. Writing down expenses for a month usually reveals one or two regular wants that could become savings.

examples.title: Three kinds of expense in one household
examples.text: Priya pays ₹12,000 rent and ₹4,500 towards a two-wheeler loan every month; these are fixed. Groceries and auto fares vary between ₹9,000 and ₹12,000. Her annual insurance premium of ₹9,000 is occasional, so she sets aside ₹750 each month instead of being caught short in the renewal month.

examples.title: Finding savings in the record
examples.text: Rahul writes down every expense for one month. He finds ₹2,400 of food delivery and ₹1,100 of unused subscriptions. Cancelling two subscriptions frees ₹700 a month without changing anything he actually values.

keyTakeaways: Split expenses into fixed, variable and occasional so nothing arrives as a surprise.
Expenditure is income minus saving, so decide savings before spending.
Needs keep life running; wants can usually wait one month.
A single month of written expenses shows where money leaks.

review.notes: The income, expenditure and saving relationship is checked against RBI FAME 4th edition, Message 1. The fixed/variable/occasional split is general practice. Awaiting a named human reviewer.

quiz.question: Which list contains only fixed expenses?
options: Insurance premium, festival spending, a medical bill
quiz.explanation: Fixed expenses stay roughly the same each month. Groceries and transport vary with use, and insurance or festival costs appear only occasionally.

quiz.question: Money is tight this month. Which item is a need rather than a want?
quiz.explanation: Missing a loan instalment creates penalties and hurts your credit record. The subscription and the trip can be postponed.

quiz.question: According to RBI's budgeting message, how should saving relate to spending?
options: Save whatever is left at the end of the month
Set aside a portion of income before you spend anything
quiz.explanation: RBI's FAME material describes expenditure as income minus saving, and advises setting aside savings from income before spending.

disclaimer: General financial education, not personalised advice. Your own essential expenses depend on your household.
